challenges.name: permission-policy-calls
challenges.title: Permission policy: judge the call
challenges.description: Two tool calls proposed by CodeDev agents, with the approval record or the session they came from. Decide whether each statement about the policy's answer holds.

questions.question:
Approval issued by the support lead at t=1000 for session s-1 (support agent):
  token apr-31  tool refund_order
  args {"orderId":"o-1042","amount":349000}
  argsHash = sha256(canonicalJson(args))   expiresAt t=301000   used false

Call proposed by the model at t=4000 in session s-1, sent by the runtime with token apr-31:
  refund_order {"amount":349000,"orderId":"o-1042"}

Policy code: canonicalJson() sorts object keys at every level and removes spaces before hashing. refund_order needs a manager above 500000.

Statement: "The policy allows this call and consumes apr-31, even though the keys are in a different order from the approved call."
questions.explanation: True. canonicalJson sorts the keys before hashing, so {"amount":349000,"orderId":"o-1042"} and {"orderId":"o-1042","amount":349000} give the same argsHash: this is the call the lead approved. The token is unused, not expired (4000 < 301000), from the same session, and 349000 is under the manager limit, so the policy allows it and consumes apr-31. Canonical form exists so that key order, which JSON does not treat as meaningful and models change freely, cannot break the binding, while a different order id or amount still would. The misconception is to bind a token to the raw JSON string of the arguments and then blame the model for "changing" the call.

False. The call names no userId, so the rule has nothing to compare and the policy allows it as a read; the tool then loads cert-9912 by id alone and hands u-512's certificate to u-310. That is the confused deputy problem through a resource id instead of a user id. A policy that inspects arguments cannot know who owns cert-9912; the tool must scope its query to the session (where: { id, userId: session.userId }), so the ownership check lives where the data is. The misconception is that one argument-level user check covers every way a call can reach another learner's data.

challenges.name: permission-policy
challenges.title: Permission policy: allow, needs approval or deny
challenges.description:
The CodeDev support agent proposes tool calls; a permission policy in front of the tools decides each one. Implement canonicalJson and the PermissionPolicy class in starter.ts.

Rules, checked in this order (the first one that applies gives the answer):
1. unknown session id -> deny "unknown_session"
2. tool not in the registry -> deny "unknown_tool"
3. the session's role is in the tool's deniedRoles -> deny "role_denied"
4. args has a userId that differs from the session's userId -> deny "user_mismatch" (the user always comes from the session)
5. read tool -> allow "read"
6. the tool has managerAbove (not null) and args.amount is not a finite number > 0 -> deny "invalid_amount"
7. no token came with the call -> needs_approval "manager_approval_required" if args.amount > managerAbove, else needs_approval "approval_required"
8. token checks: never issued -> deny "invalid_token"; already consumed -> deny "token_used"; now >= expiresAt -> deny "token_expired"; issued for another session -> deny "token_wrong_session"; issued for another tool or other arguments -> deny "token_mismatch"
9. args.amount > managerAbove and the approver's role is not "manager" -> needs_approval "manager_approval_required"
10. otherwise -> allow "approved" and consume the token (return its id in consumed).

approve(approval, now) is the human path: it records a token bound to the session, the tool name and sha256(canonicalJson(args)), with expiresAt = now + ttlMs and the approver's role. Only an allow consumes a token. canonicalJson is JSON with object keys sorted at every level and no spaces (array order is kept), so key order never changes a call's identity.

Input (stdin): { tools: [{ name, permission: "read"|"write", deniedRoles, managerAbove }], sessions: [{ id, userId, role }], events } where each event is { type: "approve", at, approval: { token, sessionId, call, approverRole, ttlMs } } or { type: "call", at, sessionId, call: { name, args }, token: string|null }; at is the fake clock in ms. The runner prints one line per call: t=<at> <session> <tool>: <decision> <reason>, plus " (consumed <token>)" on an approved call.
hints: For a write call that arrives with a token, which facts about the token must all be true before the call may run, and which of them change after it runs once?

Look at what approve() stores: the token must remember the session, the tool, a hash of the canonical arguments, the approver's role, its expiry and whether it was used. decide() then walks the numbered rules in order and returns at the first match.

A similar case on other data: a coupon code bound to { cart: "c-9", total: 120 } that expires at t=5000. Redeeming it for cart c-9 with { total: 120 } at t=4000 succeeds once and marks it spent; the same code again says "spent"; at t=5000 it says "expired"; for cart c-8 it says "wrong cart" and stays unspent.

tests.name: Reads run freely; a write waits for an approval token and consumes it once
tests.expected:
t=1000 s-1 get_order: allow read
t=2000 s-1 refund_order: needs_approval approval_required
t=4000 s-1 refund_order: allow approved (consumed apr-1)
t=5000 s-1 refund_order: deny token_used

tests.name: Role denials, and a userId that is not the session's user (confused deputy)
tests.expected:
t=1000 s-2 refund_order: deny role_denied
t=2000 s-1 get_enrollments: allow read
t=3000 s-1 get_enrollments: deny user_mismatch
t=4000 s-1 delete_account: deny role_denied
t=5000 s-1 close_ticket: deny user_mismatch

tests.name: Key order, also in nested objects, does not change a call's identity; array order does

tests.name: Tokens expire at issue time + ttlMs; a rejected attempt does not consume the token
